items.content_html:
Making an ESP8266 survive in the wild

The sketch worked. That was the problem.

I had a perfectly reasonable little temperature monitor: an ESP8266, a 10k NTC thermistor on A0, an optional OLED, and code that read the sensor, posted the result to a PHP endpoint every ten minutes, and hosted a tiny status page. On my desk, with the serial monitor open and the router two meters away, it was flawless.

Then I asked the obvious question can I stick this in a shed and forget about it for a year? and actually looked at the code with that question in mind. The honest answer was no. Not even close. It would probably survive a week, maybe two, and then it would start crashing at inconvenient hours for reasons that would be miserable to diagnose remotely.

This is the story of fixing all of that, and of what happened the first time it actually ran.

The ESP8266 wants to die, and String is helping it

The ESP8266 has roughly 50 KB of usable heap. That’s the whole budget. Your WiFi stack, your TLS buffers if you’re unlucky, your web server, your JSON all of it shares that one small pool, and there is no virtual memory, no swap, no second chance.

My original code built its HTTP payload like this:

String payload = "{\"temperature\":";
payload += String(currentTemp, 2);
payload += ",\"rssi\":";
payload += String(WiFi.RSSI());

Fine. Readable. And every single += potentially allocates a new buffer, copies the old contents, and frees the old one. Do that a few hundred times a day and the heap turns into Swiss cheese. Eventually an allocation fails in the middle of something important, the CPU panics, and you get a reset reason that says Exception and tells you nothing useful. The classic symptom is a device that runs great for three days and then reboots every forty minutes, forever, until you power-cycle it.

The fix is boring and total: no String anywhere in the steady state. Everything lives in pre-allocated char arrays and gets written with snprintf. The web page which used to be a 1.5 KB concatenation now goes out in chunks from a single static buffer. In normal operation the firmware allocates exactly zero bytes per loop iteration. I can say that with confidence because I watched the free-heap number for an hour and it didn’t move by a single byte.

While I was in there I also killed WiFi.setAutoReconnect(true), which I’ve come to believe exists mostly to give people false confidence. It sometimes reconnects. Often it doesn’t. Instead the firmware now runs a proper state machine disconnected, connecting, connected, failed that gets one small step per loop iteration, with its own exponential backoff (5 seconds up to 15 minutes). The nice side effect nobody tells you about: because nothing blocks anymore, the OTA handler and the web server stay alive during a reconnect. You can reflash the device while it’s failing to reach WiFi. That has saved me more than once.

A pile of small nasties

Once the big structural problems were gone, what remained was a long tail of small things that each, individually, will ruin a remote deployment.

The ADC is noisy. The ESP8266’s analog input jitters by 3–5 LSB on its own, which on a thermistor translates to the temperature randomly jumping by half a degree. The fix is oversampling: read it 32 times, average, done. Noise drops by √32, about 5.7×, and the readings go from “nervous” to “boring”. Boring is what you want from a sensor.

Sensors glitch. Averaging handles noise but not the occasional completely insane single sample the 22 → 68 → 22 spike that would otherwise put an ugly tooth in every chart. So there’s a persistence filter: a reading that deviates by more than 10°C from the current value is held as a candidate and only accepted if three consecutive readings agree on it. A genuine rapid change still gets through within six seconds. A one-off glitch never does.

millis() overflows. At 49.7 days. Every timing comparison in the firmware is written as now - last >= interval with unsigned longs, which wraps correctly by law of the C++ standard. I also reboot every 24 hours on purpose, so in practice it never gets anywhere near the wrap but the code is correct anyway, and “correct anyway” is free.

Flash has write endurance. About 100,000 cycles. My first version wrote a boot counter to EEPROM on every boot, which sounds fine until you imagine a crash-loop writing it a thousand times a day. The final version doesn’t write flash at all during normal operation. Boot count, upload totals, reconnect count all of it lives in RTC user memory, which survives resets but not power loss. I decided that was the right trade: I get counters that persist through crashes and scheduled reboots, zero flash wear, and I accept that unplugging the device resets them. For a monitoring node, that’s obviously correct. The only thing that writes flash anymore is an OTA update, which is what flash is for.

Is some of this overkill for a thermometer? Absolutely. But the shed is a 40-minute drive away, and “overkill” is a lot cheaper than “site visit”.

The server, or: I refuse to install a framework

The other half of the project is where the data lands. I already had a bare-PHP endpoint, and I looked at the options Laravel, a Node service, InfluxDB plus Grafana, one of the dedicated IoT platforms and then I just… didn’t. It’s one small table of readings and a devices table. SQLite in WAL mode handles that without breaking a sweat, the whole database is one file I can scp off the box, and there is no daemon to babysit.

So: bare PHP 7.4, PDO, SQLite, and a single ingest endpoint that returns {"status":"ok"}. That response contract matters more than it looks the firmware doesn’t just check the HTTP status, it reads the body, because I have personally been burned by reverse proxies that return 200 OK with an application error page. If the body contains the word error, the node counts it as a failure and backs off. If it’s empty or says ok, success. Simple, and it has never once misfired.

For the dashboard I made a decision I’m slightly embarrassed by and also completely committed to: it looks like the WordPress 5.x admin panel. The 2020 one. Dark #23282d sidebar, #0073aa blue, white cards with a 1px border and that tiny box-shadow, 13px text. I spent an hour looking at sleek Tailwind dashboards and realized I didn’t want sleek, I wanted legible at 7am on a phone while half awake, and WordPress admin is exactly that. No CSS framework. One hand-written stylesheet. Chart.js from a CDN for the graphs. The whole frontend is maybe 400 lines of CSS and I know what every one of them does.

There’s a health page that flags the things I actually care about device offline more than 30 minutes, heap minimum below 10 KB, a reset reason containing “Exception” or “Watchdog”, reconnect storms and a raw log that keeps the original JSON of every reading, which is the single most useful debugging feature in the whole project.

First boot

Flashed it, pointed it at the server, opened the device’s own web page. The memory report from the build had been reassuring:

RAM:    45% used
Flash:  29% used   ← plenty of room for OTA
IRAM:   92% used  ← looks scary, is normal; the WiFi stack reserves it

And the live dashboard, 52 seconds after boot:

WiFi:      Connected, -67 dBm, channel 3
Heap:      40,344 free / 40,256 lowest ever
Uploads:   3/3 OK, 0 failures
Boot:      1   WiFi reconnects: 1

The heap-lowest being 88 bytes below the current value is the number I’m proudest of. That’s not a memory budget, that’s a flat line. No leak, no fragmentation, nothing creeping. Whatever this thing does for the next six months, that number should stay right there.

Everything that can go wrong in the first minute didn’t. The state machine connected, the backoff logic armed itself and went to sleep, the spike filter saw 32 clean samples and rejected nothing, and the server accepted every packet and rendered it in its little WordPress cosplay.

And the temperature read 50.7°C.

The sensor is lying to me

In a room. A room that is, generously, 24 degrees.

Here’s the thing about building all of this: the firmware is, I think, genuinely good. The math checks out ADC raw 781 converts to about 59°C before the calibration offset, exactly what the dashboard shows, so the code is telling the truth. It’s the world that’s wrong. Either the thermistor is thermally coupled to the ESP8266 or its voltage regulator (both run warm, and inside any kind of enclosure the ambient can easily climb 25°C above the room), or my series resistor isn’t actually 10k, or the calibration offset I carried over from the original sketch is garbage. Probably the first one.

So the project is in the funniest possible state: an industrial-grade reliability stack non-blocking state machines, exponential backoff, watchdog feeding, heap guards, spike rejection, zero flash wear wrapped around a sensor that is confidently reporting sauna conditions. The software was the easy part. The software is done. Now I get to do the actual engineering, which is putting a real thermometer next to the probe, waiting ten minutes, and admitting that physics doesn’t care about my snprintf.

I’ll fix the offset this weekend. The shed can wait it’s apparently a shed with a very reliable 50-degree thermometer in it, which is more than I could say a month ago.

If you’re building something similar, the one thing I’d tell you is this: assume the device will be unreachable, assume the WiFi is worse than you think, assume every String is a small time bomb, and assume the sensor is lying until proven otherwise. The first three are software problems with known answers. The last one is why hardware people drink.

Code’s on GitHub. Link, The calibration fix will be too, eventually.

Router: OpenWrt (homerouter)
Date: April 2026

Overview

The goal was to resolve local hostnames in the format {hostname}.h1.ehmi.se across the network (e.g. auron.h1.ehmi.se → 10.1.0.2). This was incorrectly referred to as “mDNS” but is actually local unicast DNS resolution using the existing DNS infrastructure.

Network Topology

Client
  └──▶ Pihole (10.1.1.5)          — primary DNS, ad blocking
         └──▶ AdGuard (10.1.1.2)  — secondary DNS
               └──▶ dnsmasq (10.1.1.1) — router, knows all local hosts
                     └──▶ Internet (upstream)

Subnets

Network Interface Subnet Gateway
trusted br-trusted 10.1.0.0/24 10.1.0.1
mgmt br-mgmt 10.1.1.0/24 10.1.1.1

DNS Servers

Server IP Role
dnsmasq 10.1.1.1 Router DNS, knows local hosts
AdGuard 10.1.1.2 Secondary DNS
Pihole 10.1.1.5 Primary DNS, ad blocking

Problem

Clients could not resolve local hostnames like auron.h1.ehmi.se. All DNS traffic was hijacked by a firewall rule to go to Pihole, but Pihole had no knowledge of local hosts.

Changes Made

1. OpenWrt — dnsmasq (/etc/config/dhcp)

Configured dnsmasq to serve the h1.ehmi.se domain and auto-expand hostnames from existing DHCP host entries.

uci set dhcp.@dnsmasq[0].local='/h1.ehmi.se/'
uci set dhcp.@dnsmasq[0].domain='h1.ehmi.se'
uci commit dhcp
service dnsmasq restart

Effect: dnsmasq now answers auron.h1.ehmi.se → 10.1.0.2 automatically from the static host entries already defined in /etc/config/dhcp.

2. Pihole — Conditional Forwarding

Told Pihole to forward all h1.ehmi.se queries to dnsmasq on the router instead of trying to resolve them itself.

Location: Pihole Admin → Settings → DNS → Advanced → Reverse servers

true,10.1.0.0/24,10.1.1.1,h1.ehmi.se

Effect: Pihole now correctly returns 10.1.0.2 for auron.h1.ehmi.se instead of returning its own IP (10.1.1.5).

3. AdGuard — Upstream DNS Rule

Told AdGuard to forward all h1.ehmi.se queries to dnsmasq on the router.

Location: AdGuard Admin → Settings → DNS settings → Upstream DNS servers

[/h1.ehmi.se/]10.1.1.1

Effect: AdGuard now correctly returns 10.1.0.2 for auron.h1.ehmi.se.

Verification

All three DNS servers now return the correct answer:

nslookup auron.h1.ehmi.se 10.1.1.1   →  10.1.0.2  ✅  (dnsmasq)
nslookup auron.h1.ehmi.se 10.1.1.5   →  10.1.0.2  ✅  (Pihole)
nslookup auron.h1.ehmi.se 10.1.1.2   →  10.1.0.2  ✅  (AdGuard)
nslookup auron.h1.ehmi.se            →  10.1.0.2  ✅  (default DNS)

How It Works (Flow)

Client asks: "where is auron.h1.ehmi.se?"
        ↓
DNS Hijack firewall rule → Pihole (10.1.1.5)
        ↓
Pihole: "h1.ehmi.se is forwarded to 10.1.1.1"
        ↓
dnsmasq on router: "auron is in my host list → 10.1.0.2"
        ↓
Client gets: 10.1.0.2 ✅

Existing Host Entries (from /etc/config/dhcp)

These are automatically resolvable as {name}.h1.ehmi.se:

Hostname IP MAC
birdy 10.1.1.5 00:80:64:DD:16:13
auron 10.1.0.2 6c:29:95:b7:fd:31
Pixel-6-pro 10.1.0.3 dc:e5:5b:eb:0c:30
DESKTOP-O05GPKT 10.1.0.4 54:bf:64:61:45:55
ESP-DC8109 10.1.0.6 ec:64:c9:dc:81:09
Tenda-AP 10.1.0.7 08:40:f3:49:46:f0
jack 10.1.0.21 54:67:06:8a:ed:25
nadal 10.1.0.48 c8:b1:cd:9d:59:38

(and many more defined in the router config)

What This Is NOT

This setup is not mDNS. The differences:

Feature mDNS This setup
Protocol Multicast UDP Unicast DNS
Domain .local only h1.ehmi.se (custom)
Crosses VLANs ❌ No ✅ Yes
Needs server ❌ No (peer to peer) ✅ Yes (dnsmasq)
Works here Partial (same subnet only) ✅ Fully working

Notes

  • The DNS hijack firewall rule (DNAT on port 53) forces all clients to use Pihole regardless of their configured DNS. This is why both Pihole and AdGuard needed to be configured — depending on which server a query reaches first, it must know to forward h1.ehmi.se to dnsmasq.
  • No changes were needed to client devices.
  • Adding new hosts to /etc/config/dhcp on the router will automatically make them resolvable as {name}.h1.ehmi.se with no further changes needed.

items.content_html:
Executive Summary

Production environments require a delicate balance between security and stability. While automated patching can introduce breaking changes, ignoring vulnerabilities creates risk exposure. This article presents a pragmatic approach to monitoring Docker container vulnerabilities that alerts you to new CVEs without automatically updating your production workloads.

The Problem Space

You’re running multiple Docker containers in production. One has a known CVE. The traditional approach is either continuous manual checking or automated patching. Manual checking doesn’t scale and misses critical vulnerabilities. Automated patching can break production systems during updates.

What you need is a middle path: automated detection with manual remediation control.

Solution Architecture

High-Level Design

The monitoring system operates in three stages:

Stage 1: Vulnerability Scanning A vulnerability scanner examines your container images against continuously updated CVE databases. This happens on a schedule you define.

Stage 2: Change Detection The system compares current scan results against previous scans, identifying newly discovered vulnerabilities. This prevents alert fatigue from known issues.

Stage 3: Notification When new vulnerabilities appear, the system sends alerts through your chosen channel with sufficient detail for triage and remediation planning.

Technology Stack

Trivy serves as the vulnerability scanner. Developed by Aqua Security, it’s open-source, actively maintained, and covers multiple vulnerability databases including NVD, Red Hat, Debian, Ubuntu, and Alpine security advisories.

Comparison Engine tracks scan results over time. A simple implementation uses JSON file storage with diff logic. Production systems might use Redis or a lightweight database.

Notification Layer integrates with your existing alerting infrastructure. Options include Slack webhooks, email via SMTP, PagerDuty API, or custom webhooks.

Implementation Details

Scanner Container Setup

The scanner runs as a separate container with access to the Docker socket. This allows it to enumerate and scan your running containers without requiring installation on the host system.

Required capabilities:

  • Read access to Docker socket
  • Volume mount for persistent storage of scan results
  • Network access to pull vulnerability database updates

Security considerations:

  • Docker socket access is privileged; isolate the scanner container
  • Use read-only socket access where possible
  • Consider running on a schedule rather than continuously

Scanning Strategy

Two scanning approaches exist:

Runtime Container Scanning Scans currently running containers by connecting to the Docker daemon. Advantages include seeing exactly what’s running in production. Disadvantages include missing containers that aren’t currently active.

Image Registry Scanning Scans images from your registry before deployment. Catches vulnerabilities earlier in the pipeline but may miss runtime-specific issues or configurations.

The optimal approach combines both: registry scanning during CI/CD and runtime scanning for production verification.

Change Detection Logic

The comparison engine implements differential analysis:

  1. Store each scan result with timestamp and unique identifier
  2. On new scan completion, load previous scan results
  3. Extract CVE identifiers from both scans
  4. Calculate set difference: new_cves = current_cves - previous_cves
  5. Filter by severity threshold
  6. Generate alert payload only for filtered new CVEs

Critical implementation detail: Track CVEs by identifier, not by count. A container might have 50 known vulnerabilities, but you only care about the 2 new ones discovered today.

Severity Filtering

Trivy categorizes vulnerabilities by severity: CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW, UNKNOWN.

Production monitoring typically uses one of these strategies:

Conservative: Alert on CRITICAL only

  • Lowest noise
  • Highest risk of missing important vulnerabilities
  • Suitable for mature, well-maintained images

Balanced: Alert on CRITICAL and HIGH

  • Industry standard approach
  • Manageable alert volume
  • Appropriate for most production environments

Aggressive: Alert on MEDIUM and above

  • High alert volume
  • Comprehensive coverage
  • Suitable for high-security environments or new deployments

Notification Payload Design

Effective alerts include:

  • Container name and image tag
  • Number of new vulnerabilities by severity
  • CVE identifiers with brief descriptions
  • Links to full CVE details
  • Affected packages and available fixed versions
  • Timestamp of detection

Avoid including full scan dumps in notifications. Provide summary data with links to detailed reports.

Operational Considerations

Scan Frequency

Daily scanning balances timeliness with resource consumption. Critical infrastructure might scan every 6 hours. Less critical systems can scan weekly.

The vulnerability database updates frequently, but new CVEs affecting your specific containers appear less often. Start with daily scans and adjust based on your alert volume.

State Management

Scan results must persist between runs. Three approaches:

File-based storage: Simple JSON files on mounted volumes. Suitable for single-scanner deployments.

Redis: In-memory storage with persistence. Good for distributed scanning or integration with existing Redis infrastructure.

Database: PostgreSQL or similar. Overkill for basic monitoring but useful if building comprehensive security tooling.

Alert Fatigue Prevention

Implement these mechanisms to maintain signal-to-noise ratio:

Deduplication: Don’t alert on the same CVE multiple times if it persists across scans.

Severity thresholds: Configure minimum severity levels per container based on risk profile.

Grouped notifications: Batch multiple new CVEs into single alert rather than separate messages per CVE.

Quiet periods: Suppress alerts during maintenance windows or known update periods.

Integration with Update Workflow

The monitoring system feeds into your update process:

  1. Alert fires for new CVE
  2. Security team triages severity and exploitability
  3. Update scheduled based on risk assessment
  4. Testing in staging environment
  5. Controlled production rollout
  6. Verification scan confirms vulnerability remediation

This workflow maintains control while ensuring timely response to genuine threats.

Production Deployment Pattern

Isolated Scanner Container

Run the scanner in its own container, separate from application workloads. This isolation prevents scanner issues from affecting production services and allows independent scaling.

Resource allocation: Scanning is CPU and memory intensive during execution but idle between scans. Allocate resources based on image size and number of containers.

Scheduling

Use cron-style scheduling within the scanner container or external orchestration. Kubernetes CronJobs work well for containerized environments.

Schedule during low-traffic periods to minimize resource contention. Early morning hours typically work for most applications.

Monitoring the Monitor

Implement health checks for the scanner itself:

  • Successful database updates
  • Scan completion within expected timeframes
  • Notification delivery confirmation
  • Storage capacity monitoring

The security tool must be reliable to provide security value.

Security Implications of the Scanner

The scanner requires privileged access to function effectively. This creates its own security considerations:

Docker Socket Access: Reading the Docker socket allows container enumeration and image inspection. Limit this access strictly to the scanner container. Never expose the socket to untrusted containers.

Credential Management: If scanning private registries, the scanner needs authentication credentials. Use Docker secrets or environment variables, never hardcode credentials.

Network Segmentation: The scanner pulls vulnerability databases from external sources. Ensure appropriate network policies allow this while restricting other traffic.

Advanced Patterns

Multi-Environment Monitoring

Scan development, staging, and production separately. Development might alert on all severities to catch issues early. Production focuses on CRITICAL and HIGH to reduce noise.

Compliance Reporting

Extend the system to generate compliance reports. Many frameworks require demonstrating vulnerability management processes. Store historical scan data and generate reports showing:

  • Time to remediation for discovered vulnerabilities
  • Current vulnerability posture
  • Trend analysis over time

Integration with CI/CD

Shift left by scanning during build process. Fail builds that introduce CRITICAL vulnerabilities. This prevents vulnerable containers from reaching production entirely.

The runtime scanning then serves as verification and catches vulnerabilities discovered after deployment.

Alternative Approaches

Docker Scout

Docker’s native vulnerability scanning service. Advantages include tight integration with Docker tooling and minimal setup. Disadvantages include requiring Docker subscription for team features and less flexibility in customization.

Grype

Anchore’s scanner, similar to Trivy in capability. Well-documented and actively maintained. Choice between Trivy and Grype often comes down to team preference and existing tooling.

Clair

CoreOS project now maintained by Quay team. More complex setup but integrates well with Quay registry. Suitable for organizations heavily invested in Red Hat ecosystem.

Commercial Solutions

Snyk, Aqua Security, Prisma Cloud offer comprehensive platforms including vulnerability scanning, runtime protection, and compliance features. These provide more capabilities but come with licensing costs and vendor lock-in.

Implementation Checklist

Before deploying to production:

  • Scanner container built and tested
  • Docker socket access configured with minimal permissions
  • Vulnerability database updates successfully
  • Scan results storage configured and tested
  • Change detection logic validated with test data
  • Notification channel configured and tested
  • Severity filtering tuned to prevent alert fatigue
  • Scanning schedule defined based on risk tolerance
  • Documentation created for responding to alerts
  • Update workflow integrated with existing change management
  • Scanner monitoring and health checks in place
  • Team trained on interpreting alerts and taking action

Measuring Success

Track these metrics to validate the monitoring system:

Mean Time to Detection (MTTD): How quickly new CVEs are identified after publication. Should align with your scan frequency.

Mean Time to Remediation (MTTR): How quickly vulnerabilities are patched after detection. This measures your response process, not the scanner.

False Positive Rate: How often alerts require no action. High rates indicate severity filtering needs adjustment.

Coverage: Percentage of containers regularly scanned. Should be 100% for production workloads.

Conclusion

Automated CVE monitoring without auto-patching gives you security visibility while maintaining operational control. The key is implementing reliable detection, effective filtering to prevent alert fatigue, and integration with your existing update workflow.

Start simple with basic Trivy scanning and file-based storage. Iterate based on your specific needs and alert volume. The goal is sustainable security monitoring that your team actually acts on, not a perfect system that generates too much noise to be useful.

Security is a process, not a state. This monitoring system provides the information needed to make informed decisions about when and how to update production containers. The control remains yours, but you’re no longer operating blind to emerging vulnerabilities.
