items.content_html:
A Deep Dive into Git Secret Exposure, Recovery, and Prevention

The Incident

A production environment’s .env file containing sensitive credentials was accidentally committed and pushed to a public GitHub repository. What seemed like a straightforward fix quickly escalated into a multi-layered incident affecting production services and requiring coordinated remediation across multiple systems.

This post-mortem examines the technical details, cascading failures, and systemic improvements needed to prevent similar incidents.

What Went Wrong

Primary Failure: Missing .gitignore Entry

The root cause was deceptively simple—the .env file wasn’t excluded from version control. Despite being a well-known best practice, this configuration gap allowed sensitive credentials to enter the repository.

Exposed Data:

  • Database connection strings and passwords
  • API authentication keys
  • JWT signing secrets
  • Third-party service tokens

Secondary Failure: Template File Contamination

During remediation efforts, a second exposure was discovered: the .env.example file contained actual production credentials instead of placeholder values. This meant two separate files in the repository history contained live credentials.

Tertiary Failure: Deployment Hook Design

The production deployment system used a post-receive Git hook with this critical line:

git --work-tree=$TARGET --git-dir=$GIT_DIR checkout -f $BRANCH

The -f flag force-overwrites the working directory. When data files were removed from Git tracking during cleanup, the deployment hook deleted them from production, causing service disruption.

The Recovery Process

Phase 1: Immediate Credential Rotation (Priority One)

The first action was rotating all exposed credentials:

  • Database passwords regenerated
  • API keys revoked and replaced
  • JWT secrets rotated
  • Service authentication tokens refreshed

Critical Insight: Removing files from Git doesn’t remove credentials from the internet. Any exposed secret must be treated as permanently compromised, regardless of how quickly it’s removed from the repository.

Phase 2: History Rewriting

Removing the current file isn’t enough—the credentials exist in every commit where they appeared. Git’s immutable history means they’re accessible through:

  • Commit history (git log)
  • GitHub’s cached views
  • Search engine indexing
  • Third-party Git mirrors

Tool Selection: git-filter-repo

While several tools can rewrite Git history, git-filter-repo was chosen for its safety features and performance:

# Installation
pip install git-filter-repo

# Remove sensitive files from entire history
git-filter-repo --path .env --invert-paths --force
git-filter-repo --path .env.example --invert-paths --force

Critical Gotcha: git-filter-repo removes all remotes as a safety measure to prevent accidental pushes. Remotes must be manually re-added before pushing.

Phase 3: Multi-Remote Coordination

The repository had two remotes:

  • origin - GitHub (public)
  • production - Bare repository on production server

History rewriting had to be coordinated across both:

# Re-add remotes after filter-repo
git remote add origin git@github.com:user/repo.git
git remote add production user@server:~/repo.git

# Force push to both
git push --force origin --all
git push --force production --all

Phase 4: Production Data Recovery

The deployment triggered by the force push exposed a critical flaw in the deployment hook. Production data files that were removed from Git tracking were also deleted from the filesystem.

Files Lost:

  • known_devices.json - Device tracking database
  • device_database.json - Device metadata
  • debug.log - Application logs
  • blacklisted.json - Security blocklist
  • requests.json - Request history

Recovery Method:

These files still existed in Git history before cleanup. They were restored using:

# Find the last commit containing the files
git log --all --oneline -- known_devices.json | head -1

# Restore from that commit
git checkout <commit-hash> -- known_devices.json device_database.json debug.log blacklisted.json requests.json

# Fix permissions
chown www-data:www-data *.json *.log
chmod 644 *.json *.log

Phase 5: Deployment Hook Remediation

The post-receive hook was rewritten to preserve untracked files during deployment:

#!/bin/bash
TARGET="/var/www/app"
GIT_DIR="$HOME/app.git"
BRANCH="main"

while read oldrev newrev ref
do
  if [[ $ref = refs/heads/$BRANCH ]]; then
    echo "Deploying to production..."
    
    # Backup data files before checkout
    cd $TARGET
    cp -f known_devices.json known_devices.json.bak 2>/dev/null || true
    cp -f device_database.json device_database.json.bak 2>/dev/null || true
    cp -f debug.log debug.log.bak 2>/dev/null || true
    cp -f blacklisted.json blacklisted.json.bak 2>/dev/null || true
    cp -f requests.json requests.json.bak 2>/dev/null || true
    
    # Deploy code
    git --work-tree=$TARGET --git-dir=$GIT_DIR checkout -f $BRANCH
    
    # Restore data files if deleted by checkout
    [ ! -f known_devices.json ] && mv -f known_devices.json.bak known_devices.json 2>/dev/null || true
    [ ! -f device_database.json ] && mv -f device_database.json.bak device_database.json 2>/dev/null || true
    [ ! -f debug.log ] && mv -f debug.log.bak debug.log 2>/dev/null || true
    [ ! -f blacklisted.json ] && mv -f blacklisted.json.bak blacklisted.json 2>/dev/null || true
    [ ! -f requests.json ] && mv -f requests.json.bak requests.json 2>/dev/null || true
    
    # Cleanup
    rm -f *.bak
    
    # Fix permissions
    chown www-data:www-data $TARGET/*.json $TARGET/*.log 2>/dev/null || true
    chmod 644 $TARGET/*.json $TARGET/*.log 2>/dev/null || true
    chown www-data:www-data $TARGET/.env 2>/dev/null || true
    chmod 600 $TARGET/.env 2>/dev/null || true
    
    echo "Deployment complete!"
  fi
done

Technical Lessons

1. Git History Is Immutable (Until It Isn’t)

Git’s design philosophy treats history as immutable, which is excellent for collaboration but catastrophic for secrets. Once committed, credentials are:

  • Permanently in history until explicitly removed
  • Replicated to all clones
  • Potentially cached by GitHub
  • Possibly indexed by search engines

The Fix: History rewriting is possible but destructive. It changes all commit hashes, breaks existing clones, and requires force-pushing—a coordinated operation that can’t be done quietly.

2. .gitignore Is Not Retroactive

Adding .env to .gitignore after it’s been committed does nothing. The file remains in history. .gitignore only affects future operations.

Correct Workflow:

# Add to .gitignore FIRST
echo ".env" >> .gitignore
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "ignore environment files"

# THEN create .env
touch .env
# File is now ignored

3. Template Files Need Sanitization

.env.example files serve as templates for other developers. They should contain:

# WRONG - Real credentials
DB_PASSWORD=MyActualPassword123
API_KEY=sk_live_abc123xyz789

# RIGHT - Placeholders
DB_PASSWORD=your_secure_password_here
API_KEY=your_api_key_here

4. Deployment Hooks Must Account for State

Git tracks code, not state. Production systems often have files that shouldn’t be in Git:

  • User-uploaded content
  • Generated caches
  • Runtime logs
  • Session data
  • Application-managed databases

Deployment scripts that blindly overwrite the working directory will destroy this state.

Better Approaches:

Option A: Separate state directory

/var/www/app/        # Git-managed code
/var/www/app-data/   # Application state

Option B: Explicit exclusions

# Only checkout tracked files, preserve untracked
git checkout -f $BRANCH

Option C: Backup and restore (shown above)

5. Multi-Remote Force Push Coordination

When pushing to multiple remotes, history must be synchronized:

# This creates divergent histories (BAD)
git push --force origin main
# Make more changes
git push --force production main

# This keeps them synchronized (GOOD)
git push --force origin main
git push --force production main
# Both remotes now have identical history

6. File Ownership in Deployment Hooks

The deployment hook runs as the SSH user, but web files need different ownership:

# Wrong - Files owned by deployment user
git checkout -f $BRANCH

# Right - Explicitly set ownership
git checkout -f $BRANCH
chown -R www-data:www-data $TARGET

Prevention Strategy

Layer 1: Pre-Commit Prevention

Git Hooks:

Create .git/hooks/pre-commit:

#!/bin/bash
if git diff --cached --name-only | grep -E '^\.env$|^\.env\..*'; then
    echo "Error: Attempting to commit .env file"
    echo "Add to .gitignore instead"
    exit 1
fi

Make executable:

chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit

Automated Tools:

  • git-secrets - Scans for patterns matching credentials
  • detect-secrets - Pre-commit hook for secret detection
  • gitleaks - SAST tool for hardcoded secrets

Layer 2: Repository Configuration

Comprehensive .gitignore:

# Environment files
.env
.env.*
!.env.example

# Application state
*.log
*.json
!package.json
!composer.json

# Server configuration
.htaccess
php.ini

# Uploads
uploads/
storage/

# Caches
cache/
tmp/

Branch Protection:

Enable on GitHub:

  • Require pull request reviews
  • Require status checks
  • Restrict force pushes
  • Require signed commits

Layer 3: Secrets Management

Never Store Secrets in Git:

Use dedicated secret management:

  • HashiCorp Vault - Enterprise secret storage
  • AWS Secrets Manager - Cloud-native secrets
  • Azure Key Vault - Microsoft ecosystem
  • Google Secret Manager - GCP integration

Environment Variable Injection:

# Deploy-time injection
export DB_PASSWORD=$(vault read -field=password secret/db)
php artisan serve

Layer 4: Monitoring and Detection

GitHub Scanning:

  • Enable GitHub secret scanning (free for public repos)
  • Configure custom patterns for proprietary secrets
  • Set up notifications for detected secrets

Audit Logging:

Monitor for:

  • Unexpected credential usage from new IPs
  • API key usage spikes
  • Failed authentication attempts
  • Credential rotation events

Layer 5: Incident Response Preparation

Runbook for Credential Exposure:

  1. Immediate (0-5 minutes)

    • Rotate all exposed credentials
    • Verify rotation completed successfully
    • Monitor for unauthorized access

  2. Short-term (5-30 minutes)

    • Assess scope of exposure
    • Check logs for credential usage
    • Notify stakeholders if needed

  3. Medium-term (30 minutes - 2 hours)

    • Remove from Git history
    • Force push to all remotes
    • Verify removal from GitHub cache

  4. Long-term (2+ hours)

    • Review security logs for 30 days
    • Conduct post-mortem
    • Implement additional controls

Architecture Improvements

Separate Deployment from State

Before:

/var/www/app/
├── .env                  # Mixed: config
├── index.php             # Deployed: code
├── dashboard.php         # Deployed: code
├── known_devices.json    # State: data
└── requests.json         # State: data

After:

/var/www/app/             # Git-deployed code only
├── index.php
├── dashboard.php
└── includes/

/var/www/app-config/      # Server-managed config
├── .env
└── config.php

/var/www/app-data/        # Application state
├── known_devices.json
├── requests.json
└── logs/

Update application to load from separate paths:

// Load config from separate directory
$dotenv = Dotenv\Dotenv::createImmutable('/var/www/app-config');
$dotenv->load();

// Store data in separate directory
$dataPath = '/var/www/app-data/';

Production-Only Files Strategy

For files that must exist in production but not GitHub:

Option A: Template + Manual Creation

# In repo: .env.example
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_NAME=database_name
DB_PASSWORD=your_password_here

# On server: Copy and fill
cp .env.example .env
nano .env  # Fill with real values

Option B: Injection Script

#!/bin/bash
# deploy-inject-config.sh

# Create .env from secure storage
cat > /var/www/app/.env << EOF
DB_HOST=$(vault read -field=host secret/db)
DB_NAME=$(vault read -field=name secret/db)
DB_PASSWORD=$(vault read -field=password secret/db)
EOF

chmod 600 /var/www/app/.env
chown www-data:www-data /var/www/app/.env

Add to post-receive hook:

# After checkout
git --work-tree=$TARGET --git-dir=$GIT_DIR checkout -f $BRANCH

# Inject config
bash $HOME/deploy-inject-config.sh

The Cost of This Incident

Time Investment

  • Detection to rotation: 10 minutes
  • Total remediation: 60 minutes
  • Documentation: 120 minutes
  • Process improvements: 180 minutes

Total: ~6 hours of engineering time

Service Impact

  • Downtime: 60 minutes
  • Degraded service: 30 minutes
  • User impact: All production users

Security Impact

  • Credential exposure window: 15-30 minutes
  • Rotation completed: Yes
  • Unauthorized access detected: No
  • Long-term monitoring: Ongoing

Key Takeaways

  1. Secrets in Git are permanently exposed - History rewriting is complex, risky, and doesn’t guarantee the secret wasn’t already harvested.

  2. Credential rotation is non-negotiable - Even if you remove credentials from Git in 30 seconds, treat them as compromised.

  3. Deployment automation needs safety rails - Hooks that blindly overwrite filesystems will eventually destroy production state.

  4. Prevention is cheaper than remediation - A pre-commit hook takes 5 minutes to implement; this incident consumed 6 hours.

  5. Template files need the same security rigor - .env.example with real credentials is just as dangerous as .env.

  6. Multi-layer security is essential - No single control prevents this incident. Pre-commit hooks, .gitignore, secret scanning, and proper architecture all contribute.

  7. State and code should be separated - Mixing deployed code with runtime state creates deployment complexity and data loss risks.

  8. Force push operations require planning - When rewriting history across multiple remotes, coordination prevents divergent histories and lost work.

Conclusion

This incident demonstrates how a simple configuration oversight can cascade into a complex, multi-system remediation effort. The mistake wasn’t just committing the .env file—it was the absence of defensive layers that would have prevented or quickly caught the error.

Modern development requires defense in depth:

  • Prevent: Pre-commit hooks, gitignore templates, secret scanning
  • Detect: GitHub secret scanning, audit logs, monitoring
  • Respond: Runbooks, rotation procedures, communication plans
  • Recover: Backup strategies, deployment safety, state management

The best incident is the one that never happens. Invest in prevention now, because credential rotation at 2 AM is significantly more expensive than a 5-minute pre-commit hook setup.

Resources:

  • git-filter-repo documentation
  • GitHub Secret Scanning
  • OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet
  • The Twelve-Factor App: Config

This post-mortem is shared for educational purposes. The technical details and lessons learned are real.

items.title: WebAssembly
items.summary: WebAssembly (Wasm) is a modern, powerful technology that’s very much alive and growing! It’s quite different from Java Applets and ClickOnce - think of it as a way to run near-native speed code directly in your web browser. WebAssembly is a binary instruction format that…
items.content_html:
WebAssembly (Wasm) is a modern, powerful technology that’s very much alive and growing! It’s quite different from Java Applets and ClickOnce - think of it as a way to run near-native speed code directly in your web browser.

What is WebAssembly?

WebAssembly is a binary instruction format that runs in modern web browsers alongside JavaScript. It allows you to compile code from languages like C, C++, Rust, C#, and others to run at near-native speed in the browser.

Key Features:

  • Fast execution - Near-native performance (much faster than JavaScript for compute-heavy tasks)
  • Safe - Runs in the same sandbox as JavaScript
  • Cross-platform - Works in all modern browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge)
  • Language agnostic - Write in C++, Rust, C#, Go, etc., compile to Wasm
  • Works with JavaScript - Can call JavaScript functions and vice versa

Real-World Examples You Can Try Right Now:

Let me find some publicly available WebAssembly applications:Perfect! Here are publicly available WebAssembly applications you can try right now:

🎮 Live WebAssembly Demos You Can Use:

1. Figma - https://www.figma.com

Design tool that uses WebAssembly to achieve native-like desktop app performance in the browser

2. Google Earth - https://earth.google.com/web/

Runs entirely in the browser powered by WebAssembly

3. AutoCAD Web - https://web.autocad.com/

AutoCAD’s 35-year-old C++ application compiled to WebAssembly for the web

4. Sandspiel - https://sandspiel.club/

A falling sand game written in Rust/WebAssembly with around 2 million monthly page views

5. Qt WebAssembly Demos - https://www.qt.io/qt-examples-for-webassembly

Interactive demos including sprite drawing apps with menus, toolbars, save/load functionality, and 3D showcases

6. Felgo WASM Demos - https://felgo.com/try-wasm/

Includes weather apps, games like OneCard, and UI showcases that run directly in your browser

7. Made With WebAssembly - https://madewithwebassembly.com/

A showcase featuring production apps including uBlock Origin browser extension, OpenCascade CAD library, and PDF editors

Quick Comparison: WebAssembly vs Others

Feature WebAssembly Java Applets ClickOnce
Status ✅ Active & growing ❌ Dead (2017) ⚠️ Declining
Platform All browsers Java plugin Windows only
Performance Near-native speed Moderate Native
Security Sandboxed Vulnerable Sandboxed
Languages C++, Rust, C#, Go, etc. Java only .NET only
Installation None needed Plugin required Desktop install

Why WebAssembly is Winning:

  1. No plugins needed - runs natively in modern browsers
  2. Fast - near-native performance for compute-heavy tasks
  3. Secure - sandboxed execution
  4. Universal - works on desktop, mobile, all platforms
  5. Multi-language - write in your preferred language

Try visiting Figma or Google Earth right now - they’re full production apps running WebAssembly in your browser!

Would you like me to show you how to create your own simple WebAssembly app?

What this demo shows:

  • Real-time pixel manipulation (grayscale, invert, blur, pixelate effects)
  • Processing hundreds of thousands of pixels in milliseconds
  • Performance metrics showing processing time
  • The kind of operations where WebAssembly shines

Try the filters - click the buttons to see instant image processing!

Want to See REAL WebAssembly Code?

Here’s what actual Rust → WebAssembly code looks like:## How to Build & Use This:

1. Install Rust & wasm-pack:

curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
cargo install wasm-pack

2. Create project:

cargo new --lib my-wasm-project
cd my-wasm-project

3. Add to Cargo.toml:

[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib"]

[dependencies]
wasm-bindgen = "0.2"

4. Build:

wasm-pack build --target web

5. Use in HTML:

<script type="module">
    import init, { grayscale } from './pkg/my_wasm_project.js';
    
    await init();
    
    // Now you can call the Rust function!
    const imageData = ctx.getImageData(0, 0, 800, 600);
    grayscale(imageData.data);
    ctx.putImageData(imageData, 0, 0);
</script>

The beauty of WebAssembly is that this Rust code runs at near-native C++ speed in your browser - typically 10-20x faster than equivalent JavaScript for compute-heavy tasks!

items.title: Fixing Traefik v3 Encoded Character Blocking with Pi-hole
items.summary: If you’re running Pi-hole behind Traefik v3 as a reverse proxy, you may encounter a frustrating error when trying to manage regex-based domain blocking rules. The Pi-hole web interface returns a 400 Bad Request error, and your Traefik logs show messages like: Rejecting request because…
items.content_html:
If you’re running Pi-hole behind Traefik v3 as a reverse proxy, you may encounter a frustrating error when trying to manage regex-based domain blocking rules. The Pi-hole web interface returns a 400 Bad Request error, and your Traefik logs show messages like:

Rejecting request because it contains encoded character %5C in the URL path: /api/domains/deny/regex/(%5E%7C%5C.)(cn)%24
Rejecting request because it contains encoded character %3F in the URL path: /api/domains/deny/regex/(%3Fi)vpn

This happens when you try to enable, disable, or modify domain groups that contain regex patterns in Pi-hole’s admin interface.

Why Does This Happen?

Traefik v3 introduced a security feature that blocks HTTP requests containing certain URL-encoded characters in the path. This is designed to prevent path traversal attacks and other security vulnerabilities. The blocked characters include:

  • %2F - Forward slash (/)
  • %5C - Backslash ()
  • %00 - Null character
  • %3B - Semicolon (;)
  • %25 - Percent (%)
  • %3F - Question mark (?)
  • %23 - Hash (#)

Pi-hole’s API uses regex patterns for domain blocking, and these patterns often contain special characters like (?i) for case-insensitive matching or \. for literal dots. When the Pi-hole web interface sends these patterns to the API, they’re URL-encoded (e.g., \ becomes %5C, ? becomes %3F).

Traefik v3 sees these encoded characters and rejects the request before it even reaches Pi-hole, resulting in the 400 error.

The Investigation

The issue becomes clear when comparing direct access to Pi-hole versus access through Traefik:

Works (Direct HTTP access):

curl 'http://10.1.15.10:8000/api/domains/deny/regex/(%5E%7C%5C.)(cn)%24' \
  -X PUT \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-raw '{"groups":[0,1,2,3],"comment":"cn stuff","enabled":true,"type":"deny","kind":"regex"}'

Fails (Through Traefik HTTPS):

curl 'https://pihole.example.com/api/domains/deny/regex/(%5E%7C%5C.)(cn)%24' \
  -X PUT \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-raw '{"groups":[0,1,2,3],"comment":"cn stuff","enabled":true,"type":"deny","kind":"regex"}'

The URL encoding is identical in both cases, confirming that Traefik is the culprit, not the client or Pi-hole.

The Solution

Traefik v3.2 and later versions include configuration options to allow specific encoded characters. You need to modify your Traefik static configuration file.

Step 1: Update Your traefik.yaml

Add the encodedCharacters configuration under your HTTPS entrypoint. This configuration was introduced in Traefik v3.2 and allows you to selectively permit encoded characters in URL paths.

Reference: Traefik Documentation - Request Path

entryPoints:
  web:
    address: ":80"
  websecure:
    address: ":443"
    http3: {}
    http:
      encodedCharacters:
        allowEncodedSlash: true          # %2F - Forward slash
        allowEncodedBackSlash: true      # %5C - Backslash (Required for Pi-hole)
        allowEncodedNullCharacter: true  # %00 - Null character
        allowEncodedSemicolon: true      # %3B - Semicolon
        allowEncodedPercent: true        # %25 - Percent sign
        allowEncodedQuestionMark: true   # %3F - Question mark (Required for Pi-hole)
        allowEncodedHash: true           # %23 - Hash/pound sign

api:
  dashboard: true
  insecure: true

providers:
  docker:
    exposedByDefault: false
  file:
    directory: /etc/traefik/dynamic
    watch: true

certificatesResolvers:
  cloudflare:
    acme:
      email: your-email@example.com
      storage: /letsencrypt/acme.json
      dnsChallenge:
        provider: cloudflare
        delayBeforeCheck: 90
        resolvers:
          - "1.1.1.1:53"
          - "1.0.0.1:53"

log:
  level: INFO

Important: The most critical settings for Pi-hole are:

  • allowEncodedBackSlash: true - Required for \ in regex patterns
  • allowEncodedQuestionMark: true - Required for ? in regex patterns like (?i)

All seven encoded character options are needed to fully support Pi-hole’s regex functionality.

Step 2: Verify Your Pi-hole Dynamic Configuration

Your Pi-hole dynamic configuration (pihole.yaml) should remain simple:

http:
  middlewares:
    https-redirect:
      redirectScheme:
        scheme: https
        permanent: true

  routers:
    pihole-redirect:
      rule: "Host(`pihole.example.com`)"
      entryPoints:
        - web
      middlewares:
        - https-redirect
      service: noop@internal
    
    pihole:
      rule: "Host(`pihole.example.com`)"
      entryPoints:
        - websecure
      service: pihole
      tls:
        certResolver: cloudflare

  services:
    pihole:
      loadBalancer:
        servers:
          - url: "http://pihole:80"

Step 3: Apply the Changes

Restart Traefik to apply the new configuration:

docker restart traefik

Or if using docker-compose:

docker-compose restart traefik

Step 4: Verify the Fix

Check your Traefik logs to ensure the rejection messages are gone:

docker logs traefik -f

You should no longer see messages like “Rejecting request because it contains encoded character”.

Test by trying to enable or disable a regex domain rule in Pi-hole’s web interface. It should now work without errors.

Important Security Considerations

Allowing encoded characters reduces some of Traefik’s built-in security protections against path traversal and injection attacks. Consider these points:

  1. Understand the risks: Each allowed character opens a potential attack vector if your backend doesn’t properly validate input
  2. Pi-hole validation: Pi-hole validates regex patterns, but ensure you’re running the latest version with security patches
  3. Network segmentation: Keep your Pi-hole and Traefik on a trusted internal network, not directly exposed to the internet
  4. Monitor logs: Regularly check Traefik and Pi-hole logs for suspicious activity
  5. Regular updates: Keep both Traefik and Pi-hole updated to the latest versions
  6. Alternative approach: If security is paramount, consider using the separate entrypoint method (see Alternative Solutions below) to limit the scope of allowed encoded characters

Alternative Solutions

If you prefer not to allow encoded characters globally, here are alternatives:

Option 1: Create a Separate Entrypoint for Pi-hole

entryPoints:
  web:
    address: ":80"
  websecure:
    address: ":443"
    http3: {}
  pihole-secure:
    address: ":8443"
    http3: {}
    http:
      encodedCharacters:
        allowEncodedBackSlash: true
        allowEncodedQuestionMark: true

Then update your Pi-hole router to use pihole-secure entrypoint and access Pi-hole at https://pihole.example.com:8443.

Option 2: Use Nginx as an Intermediary

Place an Nginx container between Traefik and Pi-hole:

server {
    listen 8080;
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://pihole:80;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}

Point Traefik to Nginx instead of directly to Pi-hole.

Option 3: Downgrade to Traefik v2

Traefik v2.11 doesn’t have this encoded character restriction and works with Pi-hole out of the box:

services:
  traefik:
    image: traefik:v2.11

Common Pitfalls

YAML Indentation Errors

YAML is strict about indentation. Use spaces, not tabs. The http: section must be properly indented under websecure::

websecure:
  address: ":443"
  http3: {}
  http:              # Two spaces
    encodedCharacters: # Four spaces
      allowEncodedBackSlash: true # Six spaces

Configuration Not Loading

If you see “field not found, node: encodedPath” errors, you’re using an older Traefik version or incorrect syntax. The encodedCharacters configuration was introduced in Traefik v3.2. Check your version:

docker exec traefik traefik version

Changes Not Taking Effect

After modifying traefik.yaml, you must restart Traefik. Simply reloading dynamic configuration isn’t enough for static configuration changes.

Testing Your Configuration

After applying the fix, test with a real curl command:

curl 'https://pihole.example.com/api/domains/deny/regex/(%3Fi)vpn' \
  -X PUT \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json; charset=UTF-8' \
  -H 'Cookie: sid=YOUR_SESSION_ID' \
  -H 'X-CSRF-TOKEN: YOUR_CSRF_TOKEN' \
  --data-raw '{"groups":[0],"comment":"test","enabled":false,"type":"deny","kind":"regex"}'

A successful response (200 OK) indicates the fix is working.

Conclusion

The encoded character blocking in Traefik v3 is a security feature that can interfere with legitimate applications like Pi-hole that use special characters in their API paths. By carefully configuring the encodedCharacters settings in your Traefik static configuration, you can allow Pi-hole to function properly while maintaining reasonable security.

Remember to only enable the specific encoded characters you need, keep your systems updated, and ensure your backend applications properly validate input.

Additional Resources

  • Traefik v3 Documentation
  • Traefik Request Path Documentation
  • Pi-hole Documentation
  • Traefik GitHub Repository

Article last updated: December 2025 for Traefik v3.6.5 and Pi-hole v5 *

items.title: Fixing UEFI Shell Boot Issues on Chromebook with MrChromebox Firmware
items.summary: If you’ve installed Debian 12 on your Chromebook using MrChromebox BIOS firmware and suddenly find yourself dropped into a UEFI shell instead of your operating system, don’t panic. This is a common issue that occurs when the UEFI firmware cannot locate the bootloader on your…
items.content_html:
If you’ve installed Debian 12 on your Chromebook using MrChromebox BIOS firmware and suddenly find yourself dropped into a UEFI shell instead of your operating system, don’t panic. This is a common issue that occurs when the UEFI firmware cannot locate the bootloader on your SSD.

The error message typically indicates that the system is “booting from SSD” and asking you to “verify it contains 64bit UEFI OS.” This guide will walk you through both a quick temporary fix to boot your system immediately and a permanent solution to prevent this from happening again.

Understanding the Problem

When you see the UEFI shell, it means that the firmware has successfully detected your SSD but cannot find or execute the bootloader. This usually happens because:

  • The boot entry in NVRAM has been lost or corrupted
  • The EFI partition is not properly configured
  • GRUB bootloader files are missing or misconfigured

Quick Temporary Fix: Manual Boot from UEFI Shell

This method will get you back into your Debian system right away without making any permanent changes.

Step 1: Identify Your Drive

In the UEFI shell, type the following command to list all available filesystems:

map

This will display a list of available drives. Look for your SSD, which is typically labeled as FS0: or FS1:. Make note of which filesystem corresponds to your installation drive.

Step 2: Navigate to Your Drive

Once you’ve identified your drive, navigate to it by typing:

FS0:

Replace FS0: with whatever identifier corresponds to your SSD from the previous step.

Step 3: Boot the System

Now execute the GRUB bootloader manually:

cd EFI\debian
grubx64.efi

This should immediately boot your Debian installation. However, this is only a temporary solution, and you’ll need to repeat these steps every time you restart unless you apply the permanent fix below.

Permanent Solution: Repair Boot Entry

Once you’ve successfully booted into Debian using the method above, follow these steps to permanently fix the boot configuration.

Step 1: Check Current Boot Entries

Open a terminal and run:

sudo efibootmgr -v

This command displays all boot entries stored in your system’s NVRAM. Review the output to see if a Debian entry exists and whether it’s pointing to the correct location.

Step 2: Reinstall GRUB

Reinstall GRUB to recreate the proper boot entry:

sudo grub-install --target=x86_64-efi --efi-directory=/boot/efi --bootloader-id=debian

This command installs the GRUB bootloader to your EFI partition and creates a new boot entry in NVRAM.

Step 3: Update GRUB Configuration

After reinstalling GRUB, update its configuration:

sudo update-grub

This regenerates the GRUB configuration file with all available operating systems and kernel versions.

Step 4: Reboot and Test

Restart your system to verify that it now boots correctly:

sudo reboot

Your Chromebook should now boot directly into Debian without dropping into the UEFI shell.

Troubleshooting: EFI Partition Issues

If the above steps don’t resolve your issue, the problem might be with your EFI partition mounting.

Check if EFI Partition is Mounted

Run this command to check if your EFI partition is properly mounted:

mount | grep efi

If you don’t see any output, your EFI partition is not mounted.

Mount the EFI Partition

Identify your EFI partition (usually the first partition on your drive):

sudo fdisk -l

Look for a small partition (typically 100-500MB) with type “EFI System.”

Mount it manually:

sudo mount /dev/sda1 /boot/efi

Note: Replace /dev/sda1 with your actual EFI partition identifier from the fdisk output.

Retry GRUB Installation

Now that the EFI partition is mounted, repeat the GRUB installation steps:

sudo grub-install --target=x86_64-efi --efi-directory=/boot/efi --bootloader-id=debian
sudo update-grub

Prevention: Make EFI Partition Mount Permanent

To ensure your EFI partition always mounts at boot, verify it’s in your /etc/fstab file:

cat /etc/fstab | grep efi

If there’s no entry, add one by editing the fstab file:

sudo nano /etc/fstab

Add a line similar to:

UUID=XXXX-XXXX  /boot/efi  vfat  umask=0077  0  1

Replace XXXX-XXXX with your EFI partition’s UUID, which you can find using:

sudo blkid | grep vfat

Conclusion

The UEFI shell issue on Chromebooks running MrChromebox firmware is typically caused by missing or corrupted boot entries. By manually booting through the UEFI shell and then reinstalling GRUB from within Debian, you can restore proper boot functionality.

If you continue experiencing issues after following this guide, consider checking the MrChromebox community forums or the Chromebook-specific Linux communities for additional support related to your specific Chromebook model.

items.title: Building a Unified Deployment Pipeline: Merging Three Applications into One Coherent Site
items.summary: This article documents the architectural decisions and implementation strategies employed in consolidating three distinct web applications. a Next.js portfolio, a React-based tools suite, and a Publii blog into a unified deployment pipeline. The solution leverages GitHub Actions for automated builds, Git submodules for modular component…
items.content_html:
This article documents the architectural decisions and implementation strategies employed in consolidating three distinct web applications. a Next.js portfolio, a React-based tools suite, and a Publii blog into a unified deployment pipeline. The solution leverages GitHub Actions for automated builds, Git submodules for modular component management, and Cloudflare Pages for hosting, whilst maintaining separation of concerns and independent development workflows.

1. Introduction

Modern web development often necessitates the integration of multiple applications under a single domain, presenting unique challenges in build orchestration, routing, and deployment. This project addresses these challenges by implementing a streamlined continuous deployment workflow that preserves the autonomy of individual components whilst presenting them as a cohesive user experience.

1.1 Project Structure

The architecture comprises three principal components:

  • Portfolio (/): A Next.js application serving as the primary landing page and professional showcase
  • Tools (/tools): A React single-page application providing utility features
  • Blog (/blog): A Publii-generated static blog with independent content management

2. Technical Implementation

2.1 Repository Architecture

The project employs Git submodules to maintain independent repositories for each component, allowing for:

  • Isolated version control and commit history
  • Independent development cycles
  • Simplified testing and debugging
  • Clear separation of concerns
main-site/
├── portfolio/      (submodule)
├── tools/          (submodule)
└── blog/           (submodule, blog branch)

2.2 Build Pipeline

The deployment workflow, triggered manually via GitHub Actions, executes the following sequence:

  1. Checkout Phase: Retrieves all repositories with their submodules, ensuring the blog submodule switches to its dedicated blog branch
  2. Build Phase: Compiles both Node.js applications independently, with the tools application configured for a /tools base path
  3. Integration Phase: Constructs a unified directory structure by copying built assets to their respective paths
  4. Deployment Phase: Commits the compiled assets to a production branch, ready for hosting

2.3 Routing and Configuration

Three critical configuration files manage site behaviour:

robots.txt: Directs search engine crawlers to appropriate sitemaps for each section

sitemap.xml: Provides a sitemap index coordinating discovery across all three applications

_redirects: Handles legacy subdomain redirects and single-page application routing for the tools section

3. Key Design Decisions

3.1 Submodule Strategy

Rather than employing a monorepo approach, Git submodules were selected for their ability to maintain truly independent repositories. This proves particularly valuable when components require different deployment schedules or have distinct contributor teams.

3.2 Build-Then-Deploy Pattern

The workflow performs all compilation in the CI environment rather than on the hosting platform. This approach offers several advantages:

  • Predictability: Builds occur in a controlled environment with consistent dependencies
  • Flexibility: Different build tools and Node versions can be employed per component
  • Speed: The hosting platform simply serves pre-built assets without compilation overhead
  • Security: Build secrets and dependencies remain within the CI environment

3.3 Branch-Based Deployment

Deploying to a dedicated production branch, rather than directly to main, provides:

  • Clean separation between source code and compiled assets
  • Simplified hosting configuration (point to branch root)
  • Ability to inspect deployed assets independently
  • Protection of source branches from build artifacts

4. Challenges and Solutions

4.1 SPA Routing

Single-page applications like the React tools require special routing considerations. The _redirects file instructs Cloudflare Pages to serve index.html for all /tools/* paths, enabling client-side routing whilst avoiding 404 errors.

4.2 Blog Branch Management

The blog submodule maintains content on a separate blog branch to distinguish between Publii’s generated output and its configuration files. The workflow explicitly checks out this branch, ensuring the correct content is deployed.

4.3 Path Consistency

React’s build process required configuration via the PUBLIC_URL environment variable to ensure asset paths reference /tools rather than the root. This prevents broken links and ensures proper resource loading.

5. Recommendations and Best Practices

5.1 For Similar Projects

If you’re considering a similar architecture, I’d advise:

  • Start Simple: Begin with manual deployment to understand the full picture before automating
  • Test Independently: Ensure each component builds and runs correctly in isolation before integration
  • Document Paths: Maintain clear documentation of which files live where, particularly when using submodules
  • Version Lock: Pin Node versions and major dependencies to avoid unexpected build failures

5.2 Potential Improvements

Whilst the current solution proves effective, several enhancements could be considered:

  • Automated Testing: Integrate end-to-end tests before deployment to catch broken links or routing issues
  • Preview Deployments: Implement branch-based preview deployments for testing changes before production
  • Cache Optimisation: Investigate caching strategies to reduce build times for unchanged components
  • Monitoring: Add deployment notifications and uptime monitoring

5.3 When Not to Use This Approach

This architecture may not suit all scenarios. Consider alternatives if:

  • Components require frequent coordinated updates (a monorepo might be preferable)
  • Your team lacks familiarity with Git submodules (they can be tricky)
  • You need server-side rendering or dynamic routes (static hosting has limitations)
  • Build times become prohibitive (incremental builds might be necessary)

6. Conclusion

This unified deployment pipeline successfully consolidates three independent applications whilst preserving their modularity and independence. The solution demonstrates that with careful planning and appropriate tooling, complex multi-application sites can be managed through automated workflows without sacrificing simplicity or maintainability.

The key takeaway is that modern deployment needn’t be monolithic. By combining Git submodules, GitHub Actions, and intelligent routing configuration, we can achieve the best of both worlds: the organisational benefits of separate repositories with the user experience of a unified site.

The complete workflow requires minimal ongoing maintenance. simply trigger the action when updates are ready, and the pipeline handles the rest. It’s rather elegant in its simplicity, really.

Technical Stack: Next.js, React, Publii, GitHub Actions, Cloudflare Pages
Repository Structure: Git submodules with independent version control
Deployment Target: Static hosting with SPA routing support
Build Time: Approximately 3-5 minutes for full deployment

items.title: Constructing a Minimal 12MB Operating System for Web Hosting: A Comprehensive Technical Guide
items.summary: This article presents a methodical approach to engineering a lightweight operating system, constrained to approximately 12 megabytes, specifically designed for Internet connectivity and web server deployment. This endeavour demonstrates the viability of creating functional networked systems without the bloat associated with contemporary operating systems, whilst…
items.content_html:
This article presents a methodical approach to engineering a lightweight operating system, constrained to approximately 12 megabytes, specifically designed for Internet connectivity and web server deployment. This endeavour demonstrates the viability of creating functional networked systems without the bloat associated with contemporary operating systems, whilst maintaining sufficient capability to serve web content reliably.

1. Introduction and Rationale

The Contemporary Problem

Modern operating systems, Linux distributions, Windows, macOS, typically consume several gigabytes of storage. For embedded systems, IoT devices, or legacy hardware with severely limited resources, this represents an unrealistic proposition. The question thus arises: what constitutes the absolute minimum viable system capable of connecting to the Internet and hosting a functional web server?

Our Objective

We shall construct an operating system that fulfils the following requirements:

  • Total footprint: approximately 12 megabytes
  • Core functionality: networking capabilities and HTTP server functionality
  • Deployment: bootable via QEMU or physical hardware
  • Architecture: x86-64 compatible for broad hardware support

This represents a reduction of approximately 99.9% compared to typical Linux distributions.

2. Architectural Overview

Component Breakdown

A functional operating system comprises four essential components:

Component Size Purpose
Bootloader ~0.5 MB Initial system initialisation and kernel loading
Linux Kernel 4–6 MB Core system, networking, and device management
Busybox 1–2 MB Essential command-line utilities and init system
Root Filesystem <1 MB Configuration files, web content, system directories

Total: approximately 12 MB

Design Philosophy

The approach adheres to the Unix principle of doing one thing exceedingly well. Rather than attempting to build an operating system from scratch, a Herculean undertaking, we leverage established, well-tested components and strip them to their essentials.

3. Preparation and Environment Setup

Prerequisites

Before commencing, ensure your development system possesses:

  • A Linux-based development environment (Ubuntu, Debian, or similar)
  • Approximately 2–3 gigabytes of free disk space for compilation artefacts
  • Essential build tools: gcc, make, git, wget
  • Moderate technical proficiency with command-line interfaces

Establishing the Build Environment

# Install requisite dependencies
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install build-essential wget git bc ncurses-dev \
  flex bison openssl libssl-dev libelf-dev libdw-dev \
  binutils-dev nasm mtools qemu-system-x86

# Establish project directory structure
mkdir -p ~/minimal-os/{kernel,busybox,syslinux,rootfs/{boot,www,etc,proc,sys,dev}}
cd ~/minimal-os

This foundational step ensures all necessary tools are available for subsequent compilation tasks.

4. Linux Kernel Compilation

Kernel Selection and Download

The Linux kernel, the heart of any Linux-based operating system, must be compiled with minimal configuration to reduce its footprint.

cd ~/minimal-os/kernel
wget https://www.kernel.org/pub/linux/kernel/v6.x/linux-6.1.158.tar.xz
tar xf linux-6.1.158.tar.xz
cd linux-6.1.158

Kernel Configuration Strategy

Rather than including drivers for every conceivable device, we shall configure the kernel exclusively for:

  • Networking capabilities (essential for Internet connectivity)
  • Virtual block devices (e.g., SATA, virtio for QEMU compatibility)
  • ext4 filesystem support
  • Serial console output (invaluable for debugging)
# Generate minimal configuration
cat > .config << 'EOF'
CONFIG_64BIT=y
CONFIG_X86=y
CONFIG_KERNEL_GZIP=y
CONFIG_SERIAL_8250=y
CONFIG_SERIAL_8250_CONSOLE=y
CONFIG_NET=y
CONFIG_INET=y
CONFIG_NETDEVICES=y
CONFIG_NET_CORE=y
CONFIG_E1000=y
CONFIG_VIRTIO_NET=y
CONFIG_EXT4_FS=y
CONFIG_SYSVIPC=n
CONFIG_SYSFS=y
CONFIG_PROC_FS=y
CONFIG_DEVTMPFS=y
CONFIG_DEVTMPFS_MOUNT=y
CONFIG_UNIX=y
CONFIG_MODULES=n
CONFIG_DEBUG_KERNEL=n
CONFIG_STRIP_ASM_SYMS=y
EOF

# Populate remaining configuration with sensible defaults
make olddefconfig

# Initiate compilation
make -j$(nproc)

# Verify kernel size
ls -lh arch/x86/boot/bzImage

Expected outcome: A kernel binary of 4–6 MB.

Compilation Considerations

The -j$(nproc) flag parallelises compilation across available CPU cores, significantly reducing compilation time. On modern hardware, anticipate 10–30 minutes of compilation time.

Advisory note: Should compilation failures occur, ensure all prerequisite libraries are installed. The libelf-dev and libdw-dev packages are frequently overlooked yet essential.

5. Busybox: The Swiss Army Knife

Understanding Busybox

Busybox consolidates numerous Unix utilities into a single, statically-linked binary. Rather than maintaining separate executables for ls, cat, cp, et cetera, Busybox provides all functionality within approximately 1–2 megabytes.

Busybox Configuration

cd ~/minimal-os/busybox
wget https://busybox.net/downloads/busybox-1.36.1.tar.bz2
tar xf busybox-1.36.1.tar.bz2
cd busybox-1.36.1

# Apply minimal configuration
cat > .config << 'EOF'
CONFIG_SH_ASH=y
CONFIG_INIT=y
CONFIG_MOUNT=y
CONFIG_UMOUNT=y
CONFIG_HOSTNAME=y
CONFIG_IFCONFIG=y
CONFIG_PING=y
CONFIG_ROUTE=y
CONFIG_DHCPC=y
CONFIG_WGET=y
CONFIG_HTTPD=y
CONFIG_HTTPD_PORT=80
CONFIG_LS=y
CONFIG_CP=y
CONFIG_MV=y
CONFIG_RM=y
CONFIG_MKDIR=y
CONFIG_CAT=y
CONFIG_ECHO=y
CONFIG_FIND=y
CONFIG_STATIC=y
EOF

# Compile with static linking
make oldconfig
make -j$(nproc) LDFLAGS="-static"

# Verify binary size
ls -lh busybox

Static linking ensures the binary operates independently, without requiring shared libraries. This is critical for embedded systems.

6. Root Filesystem Construction

Directory Structure Establishment

cd ~/minimal-os/rootfs

# Create essential directories
mkdir -p {bin,sbin,etc,proc,sys,dev,var,tmp,www,boot/syslinux}

# Copy compiled binaries
cp ~/minimal-os/kernel/linux-6.1.158/arch/x86/boot/bzImage boot/kernel
cp ~/minimal-os/busybox/busybox-1.36.1/busybox bin/

# Create symbolic link
cd bin && ln -s busybox sh && cd ..

System Initialisation Scripts

# Create init script
cat > etc/init.d/rcS << 'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
mount -t proc none /proc
mount -t sysfs none /sys
mount -t devtmpfs none /dev
hostname minimal-web-server
echo "Minimal Web OS Initialising..."
ifconfig lo 127.0.0.1
udhcpc -i eth0 &
/bin/busybox httpd -h /www
EOF

chmod +x etc/init.d/rcS

# Create inittab configuration
cat > etc/inittab << 'EOF'
::sysinit:/etc/init.d/rcS
::askfirst:/bin/sh
::ctrlaltdel:/bin/umount -a -r
EOF

# System user files
cat > etc/passwd << 'EOF'
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/sh
EOF

cat > etc/group << 'EOF'
root:x:0:
EOF

Web Content

# Create sample webpage
cat > www/index.html << 'EOF'
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Minimal Web Server</title>
    <style>
        body { font-family: 'Segoe UI', Tahoma, Geneva, Verdana, sans-serif; 
               background: linear-gradient(135deg, #667eea 0%, #764ba2 100%); 
               padding: 20px; margin: 0; }
        .container { max-width: 600px; margin: 0 auto; 
                    background: white; padding: 30px; border-radius: 8px; 
                    box-shadow: 0 10px 25px rgba(0,0,0,0.2); }
        h1 { color: #333; margin-top: 0; }
        .status { background: #d4edda; color: #155724; 
                 padding: 15px; border-radius: 4px; }
        p { color: #666; line-height: 1.6; }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <div class="container">
        <h1>✓ Minimal Operating System</h1>
        <div class="status">
            <strong>Status:</strong> Web server operational
        </div>
        <p>This server is executing upon a custom-engineered minimal Linux operating system, constrained to approximately 12 megabytes.</p>
        <p><strong>System Specifications:</strong></p>
        <ul>
            <li>Total OS size: ~12 MB</li>
            <li>Kernel: Linux 6.1.158 (minimal configuration)</li>
            <li>Utilities: Busybox 1.36.1</li>
            <li>Web Server: Busybox httpd</li>
            <li>Filesystem: ext4</li>
        </ul>
    </div>
</body>
</html>
EOF

7. Bootloader Installation

Syslinux: The Boot Manager

Syslinux provides a lightweight bootloader capable of loading and executing the Linux kernel.

cd ~/minimal-os/syslinux
wget https://mirrors.edge.kernel.org/pub/linux/utils/boot/syslinux/syslinux-6.03.tar.gz
tar xf syslinux-6.03.tar.gz
cd syslinux-6.03

# Compile Syslinux
make -j$(nproc)

# Locate the bootloader binary
find . -name "syslinux.bin" -type f

Boot Configuration

cd ~/minimal-os/rootfs/boot/syslinux

cat > syslinux.cfg << 'EOF'
PROMPT 1
TIMEOUT 50
DEFAULT linux

LABEL linux
    KERNEL /boot/kernel
    APPEND root=/dev/sda1 console=ttyS0 console=tty0 quiet
EOF

8. Creating the Bootable Disk Image

Disk Image Generation

cd ~/minimal-os

# Create 12 MB raw disk image
dd if=/dev/zero of=disk.img bs=1M count=12

# Create partition table
(echo o; echo n; echo p; echo 1; echo ; echo ; echo w) | fdisk disk.img

# Establish loop device
LOOP=$(sudo losetup -f)
sudo losetup $LOOP disk.img -o 1048576

# Format partition
sudo mkfs.ext4 -F $LOOP

# Mount and populate
mkdir -p mnt
sudo mount $LOOP mnt
sudo cp -r rootfs/* mnt/
sudo sync
sudo umount mnt

# Install bootloader
SYSLINUX_BIN=$(find syslinux/syslinux-6.03 -name "syslinux.bin" -type f | head -1)
sudo dd if=$SYSLINUX_BIN of=disk.img bs=1 count=440 conv=notrunc

# Finalisation
sudo losetup -d $LOOP

# Verification
ls -lh disk.img

9. Deployment and Testing

QEMU Emulation (Recommended)

For initial testing, QEMU provides a safe, isolated environment:

qemu-system-x86_64 -drive file=disk.img,format=raw \
  -m 256 \
  -netdev user,id=net0 \
  -device e1000,netdev=net0 \
  -nographic \
  -serial mon:stdio

Expected Behaviour

Upon boot, you should observe:

  1. Bootloader initialisation via Syslinux
  2. Kernel loading and initialisation messages
  3. Network interface configuration via DHCP
  4. Web server activation on port 80
  5. System ready for incoming HTTP requests

Testing Connectivity

# From your host system (in another terminal)
# If using QEMU user networking, access at localhost

# Get IP from QEMU output, then:
curl http://192.168.x.x
# Should return your HTML page

Physical Hardware Deployment (Advanced)

Caution: This operation will overwrite your target storage device.

# Write to USB drive (replace sdX with your device)
sudo dd if=disk.img of=/dev/sdX bs=4M conv=fsync
sudo sync

10. Optimisation and Troubleshooting

Size Reduction Strategies

Should your system exceed 12 MB, consider:

  1. Binary stripping: strip ~/minimal-os/rootfs/bin/busybox
  2. Kernel compression: Enable XZ compression in CONFIG_KERNEL_XZ
  3. Minimal configuration: Disable unused Busybox utilities
  4. Filesystem optimisation: Remove unnecessary files from /var

Common Issues and Remedies

Issue Solution
Kernel fails to compile Reinstall libelf-dev, libdw-dev
Network unreachable Verify CONFIG_NETDEVICES=y and CONFIG_E1000=y
Web server won’t start Check /www/index.html exists and permissions
Boot hangs at Syslinux Verify kernel path in syslinux.cfg is correct
Filesystem corruption Regenerate disk image from scratch

11. Conclusions and Future Considerations

Achievements

Through this exercise, we have demonstrated:

  • The viability of creating functional operating systems at minimal scale
  • The efficacy of leveraging established open-source components
  • The potential for deploying systems on severely constrained hardware

Practical Applications

Such minimalist systems prove invaluable for:

  • Embedded IoT devices
  • Legacy hardware revitalisation
  • Disaster recovery and minimal boot environments
  • Educational purposes and systems programming study
  • Network-attached storage (NAS) on minimal hardware

Further Enhancements

For production deployment, one might consider:

  • Integration with Docker for containerised applications
  • Implementation of systemd for more sophisticated service management
  • SSL/TLS support for secure web communications
  • Database integration for dynamic content generation
  • Automated deployment via cloud-init or similar technologies

12. Final Remarks

The construction of a minimal operating system represents not merely a technical exercise, but a valuable reminder that contemporary bloat is not inevitable. By understanding the constituent components of an operating system and making deliberate design choices, one can create systems that are simultaneously powerful and parsimonious in their resource consumption.

This approach, building only what is necessary, remains a cornerstone principle of excellent engineering, whether applied to operating systems, software architecture, or infrastructure design.

Appendix A: Complete Build Script

For those preferring automation:

#!/bin/bash
set -e

cd ~/minimal-os

echo "=== Compiling Linux Kernel ==="
cd kernel/linux-6.1.158
make -j$(nproc)
cp arch/x86/boot/bzImage ../../../rootfs/boot/kernel

echo "=== Compiling Busybox ==="
cd ~/minimal-os/busybox/busybox-1.36.1
make -j$(nproc) LDFLAGS="-static"
cp busybox ../../rootfs/bin/
cd ../../rootfs/bin && ln -sf busybox sh

echo "=== Building Syslinux ==="
cd ~/minimal-os/syslinux/syslinux-6.03
make -j$(nproc)

echo "=== Creating Disk Image ==="
cd ~/minimal-os
dd if=/dev/zero of=disk.img bs=1M count=12
(echo o; echo n; echo p; echo 1; echo ; echo ; echo w) | fdisk disk.img

LOOP=$(sudo losetup -f)
sudo losetup $LOOP disk.img -o 1048576
sudo mkfs.ext4 -F $LOOP
mkdir -p mnt
sudo mount $LOOP mnt
sudo cp -r rootfs/* mnt/
sudo sync
sudo umount mnt

SYSLINUX_BIN=$(find syslinux/syslinux-6.03 -name "syslinux.bin" | head -1)
sudo dd if=$SYSLINUX_BIN of=disk.img bs=1 count=440 conv=notrunc
sudo losetup -d $LOOP

echo "✓ Build complete!"
ls -lh disk.img

References

  • Linux Kernel Documentation: https://www.kernel.org/doc/
  • Busybox Project: https://busybox.net/
  • Syslinux Project: https://syslinux.org/
  • QEMU Documentation: https://www.qemu.org/documentation/

items.content_html:
Introduction to Discord Webhooks

Discord has grown beyond a simple voice chat platform into a full-fledged community hub for gamers, developers, and businesses alike. One of the most powerful tools it offers is webhooks.

But what exactly are Discord webhooks, and how can you use them effectively? Whether you’re a beginner looking to send automated notifications or a developer integrating external apps, this guide will walk you through everything you need to know—complete with practical examples.

What Are Discord Webhooks?

At its core, a Discord webhook is a way for external applications to send messages into a Discord channel automatically. Instead of typing a message yourself, you can configure apps or scripts to push content directly into your server.

In simpler terms, think of webhooks as automated messengers that can deliver updates, alerts, or notifications straight into your community.

Why Use Discord Webhooks?

Some of the most common reasons people use Discord webhooks include:

  • Automated Notifications – Get alerts when a new commit is pushed on GitHub or when your server goes down.

  • Integration with External Apps – Connect platforms like Trello, GitHub, or Jenkins with your Discord server.

  • Custom Announcements – Post updates from a website, blog, or bot without manual input.

Benefits of Discord Webhooks for Developers and Communities

  • Saves time with automation

  • Improves communication in communities

  • Provides real-time monitoring (e.g., error alerts, API logs)

  • Easy to set up without coding knowledge

Setting Up a Discord Webhook

Prerequisites Before Creating a Webhook

Before you start, make sure you have:

  • A Discord server where you have Manage Webhooks permission

  • A channel where notifications will be posted

  • Basic familiarity with copy-pasting links

Step-by-Step Guide to Creating a Webhook in Discord

  1. Open Server Settings in Discord.

  2. Select Integrations → Webhooks.

  3. Click New Webhook.

  4. Give your webhook a name and assign it to a channel.

  5. Copy the Webhook URL—this is what you’ll use to send data.

Managing and Customizing Your Webhook

You can:

  • Assign an avatar (custom profile picture)

  • Change its posting channel anytime

  • Rename the webhook for different use cases

How Discord Webhooks Work Internally

Anatomy of a Webhook URL

A Discord webhook URL looks like this:

https://discord.com/api/webhooks/{webhook.id}/{webhook.token}

Both the ID and Token must be kept secure, as anyone with this link can post messages to your channel.

Supported Data Formats (JSON & Embeds)

  • Plain text messages – Quick updates

  • JSON payloads – Structured data

  • Embeds – Rich content with titles, descriptions, images, and fields

Sending Messages with Discord Webhooks

Sending a Simple Text Message via cURL

curl -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d '{"content":"Hello from Discord Webhook!"}' \
https://discord.com/api/webhooks/WEBHOOK_ID/WEBHOOK_TOKEN

Sending JSON Payloads with Custom Formatting

{
  "content": "New update available!",
  "username": "Update Bot",
  "avatar_url": "https://example.com/avatar.png"
}

Adding Embeds for Rich Content

{
  "embeds": [{
    "title": "Server Status",
    "description": "✅ All systems operational",
    "color": 65280
  }]
}

Practical Examples of Using Discord Webhooks

Example 1: GitHub Push Notifications

In your GitHub repository, go to Settings → Webhooks → Add Webhook.

Paste your Discord Webhook URL into the “Payload URL” field.

Set the Content type to application/json and choose which events you’d like (e.g., push, pull_request, or issues).

Now, whenever someone pushes new code, merges a pull request, or opens an issue, Discord will automatically post a structured message in your chosen channel.

This makes it easy for your whole team to stay up-to-date on changes without leaving Discord.

Example 2: Server Monitoring Alerts

Use free uptime monitoring services like UptimeRobot, BetterUptime, or even custom scripts running on your server.

Configure these tools to send alerts to your Discord Webhook if your website or application goes offline, response times spike, or critical errors occur.

You can customize alert frequency (e.g., every 5 minutes if downtime persists) and format the message to include server name, timestamp, and current status.

This ensures your team gets real-time alerts directly in Discord, making it easier to respond quickly without having to constantly check dashboards.

Example 3: Custom Bot-like Notifications

Even without coding a bot, Discord webhooks allow you to send styled messages using JSON payloads.

You can customize:

Username & Avatar → Make messages appear as if they came from a bot or a custom account.

Rich Embeds → Add colored sidebars, bold titles, clickable links, images, and even fields with structured data.

Timestamps → Automatically show when an event occurred.

Example: You could create a webhook that posts a daily summary like:

“✅ All systems running smoothly”

“⚠️ Warning: Disk usage at 85%”

This makes the webhook feel like a lightweight bot, perfect for dashboards, reminders, or project updates without needing to host or code a full bot.

Advanced Webhook Features

Discord webhooks may seem simple at first glance, but they offer powerful features when combined with external scripts and automation tools. Let’s break down some advanced capabilities.

Using Multiple Webhooks in One Channel

  • A single channel can have multiple webhooks assigned.

  • This is useful if you want different integrations—for example:

    • One webhook for GitHub updates

    • Another webhook for server monitoring

    • A third webhook for announcements

Pro Tip: Assign unique usernames and avatars to differentiate which webhook sent the message.

Automating Webhooks with Python or Node.js

Instead of manually using cURL, you can integrate webhooks into scripts or applications.

Example: Sending a Message with Python (using requests)

import requests

url = "https://discord.com/api/webhooks/WEBHOOK_ID/WEBHOOK_TOKEN"
data = {
    "content": "Hello from Python!",
    "username": "Python Bot"
}

response = requests.post(url, json=data)
print(response.status_code)

Example: Sending a Message with Node.js

const fetch = require("node-fetch");

const url = "https://discord.com/api/webhooks/WEBHOOK_ID/WEBHOOK_TOKEN";

const data = {
  content: "Hello from Node.js!",
  username: "Node Bot"
};

fetch(url, {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify(data)
})
.then(res => console.log(res.status));

With these, you can automate alerts, reminders, and event notifications.

Rate Limits and Best Practices

Discord webhooks are subject to rate limits to prevent spam:

  • Maximum of 5 requests per second per webhook

  • Payload size should not exceed 8 MB

Best Practices:

  • Bundle multiple messages into a single embed instead of spamming

Security Considerations for Discord Webhooks

Protecting Your Webhook URL

Anyone with your webhook URL can post messages in your channel. To secure it:

  • Store it in a safe location (e.g., .env file for projects)

  • Regenerate the webhook if you suspect it has been compromised

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Posting sensitive information (passwords, API keys) through webhooks

  • Forgetting to set the Content-Type header as application/json

  • Ignoring rate limits, which may result in failed requests

Common reasons include:

  • Invalid webhook URL (copied incorrectly)

  • Missing Content-Type header

  • JSON payload formatting errors

If Discord rejects your request, double-check:

  • Brackets {} and arrays [] are properly closed

  • Field names are lowercase (e.g., "content", not "Content")

  • Payload size does not exceed 8 MB
